core_problem: In 2023, global mean temperature surged to 1.48K above pre-industrial levels, with about 0.2K unexplained by known drivers such as anthropogenic warming and the El Niño onset.
methodology_summary: Satellite data (CERES-EBAF) and ERA5 reanalysis were used to analyze top-of-atmosphere radiative fluxes, planetary albedo, cloud cover trends, and Earth's energy imbalance, decomposing the 2023 temperature anomaly into contributions from albedo changes, incident solar radiation, and El Niño.
key_trade_off: The record warming occurred despite increasing outgoing longwave radiation (which offsets greenhouse warming), because a simultaneous record decline in planetary albedo, driven by reduced low clouds, caused an even larger increase in absorbed solar radiation.
limitations: Inability to quantitatively partition the low-cloud decline into internal variability, aerosol indirect effects, and cloud feedback.
Discrepancies between CERES and ERA5 datasets, notably in incident solar radiation anomalies.
The analysis relies on a single exceptional year (2023), making it difficult to separate forced trends from short-term variability.
Uncertainties in the magnitude of contributions from recent ship fuel regulations and other aerosol changes.
Limited insight into the spatial and process-level details of the observed cloud changes.
future_directions: Use climate models with constrained forcing to attribute low-cloud trends to internal variability, aerosol changes, and feedbacks.
Enhance satellite and reanalysis intercomparisons to reduce observational uncertainties in the radiation budget.
Monitor evolving cloud and albedo trends to determine if the 2023 decline is transient or part of a persistent feedback.
Investigate regional mechanisms, especially over the North Atlantic and tropical oceans, driving low-cloud reductions.
Assess implications for climate sensitivity estimates and likely time to exceed 1.5°C warming.
research_gaps: The relative contributions of natural variability versus anthropogenic aerosol reductions to the multi-year low-cloud decline.
The extent to which the albedo drop reflects an emerging positive cloud feedback that would accelerate future warming.
Quantification of the role of polar versus non-polar albedo changes in global shortwave absorption anomalies.
suggested_title: Attribution of the 2023 Record-Low Planetary Albedo: Internal Variability, Aerosol Forcing, and the Cloud Feedback
suggested_abstract: The surprising 2023 global temperature surge was largely driven by a record decline in planetary albedo due to reduced low-cloud cover. This study uses large ensembles of climate model simulations, historical forcing datasets, and advanced detection-attribution methods to decompose the observed low-cloud trend into components forced by aerosol changes, natural internal variability, and a possible emergent cloud feedback. Our results sharpen the estimated role of aerosols, constrain the unforced variability range, and provide critical evidence regarding the persistence of the cloud decline, with direct implications for near-term warming projections and climate sensitivity.
